column2: From Ibn ʿUmar (may Allah the Exalted be pleased with them both) that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god but Allah

and that Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah, establish the prayer and pay the zakāh. If they do that, they have protected their blood and their wealth from me, except by the right of Islam, and their reckoning is with Allah the Exalted.” Reported by al-Bukhārī and Muslim.
Al-Bukhārī and Muslim recorded this hadith in the two Ṣaḥīḥs in the narration of Wāqid ibn Muḥammad ibn Zayd ibn ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar, from his father, from his grandfather ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar.
His words “except by the right of Islam”: al-Bukhārī alone has this wording, not Muslim.
The meaning of this hadith has been narrated from the Prophet ﷺ by several routes. In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, from Anas, the Prophet ﷺ said:
“I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muḥammad is His servant and Messenger. When they testify that there is no god but Allah
and that Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah, pray our prayer, face our qiblah and eat our slaughtered meat, their blood and their wealth become inviolable to us, except by its right.”

Imam Aḥmad recorded from the hadith of Muʿādh ibn Jabal (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Prophet ﷺ said: “I have only been commanded to fight the people until they establish the prayer, pay the zakāh,

and testify that there is no god but Allah alone, without partner, and that Muḥammad is His servant and Messenger. If they do that, they have taken protection and protected their blood and their wealth, except by its right, and their reckoning is with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.”
Ibn Mājah recorded it in abridged form.

He also recorded something similar from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him); but the well-known narration of Abū Hurayrah makes no mention of establishing the prayer or paying the zakāh. In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, Abū Hurayrah reports that the Prophet ﷺ said:
“I have been commanded to fight the people until they say ‘There is no god but Allah’. Whoever says ‘There is no god but Allah’ has protected his wealth and his life from me, except by its right,
and his reckoning is with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.” In a narration of Muslim: “…until they testify that there is no god but Allah and believe in me and in what I have brought.”

Muslim also recorded it from the hadith of Jābir (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet ﷺ, in the wording of Abū Hurayrah's first hadith, adding at the end: Then he recited: “So remind; you are only a reminder. You are not a controller over them” [al-Ghāshiyah 88:21–22].

He also recorded from the hadith of Abū Mālik al-Ashjaʿī, from his father, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: “Whoever says ‘There is no god but Allah’ and disbelieves in whatever is worshipped besides Allah, his wealth and his blood become inviolable, and his reckoning is with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.”
It is narrated that Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah said: This was at the beginning of Islam, before prayer, fasting, zakāh and emigration were made obligatory. This is very weak,
and whether it is authentic from Sufyān is open to question, for the narrators of these hadiths accompanied the Prophet ﷺ only in Madīnah, and some of them embraced Islam late.

Moreover, his words “they have protected their blood and their wealth from me” show that when he said this he had been commanded to fight, and to kill whoever refused Islam — and all of that was after his emigration to Madīnah.
It is known by necessity that the Prophet ﷺ used to accept the two testimonies alone from everyone who came to him wanting to enter Islam, and by them protected his blood
and counted him a Muslim. He rebuked Usāmah ibn Zayd for killing a man who said “There is no god but Allah” when Usāmah raised the sword over him, and he rebuked him severely.

The Prophet ﷺ did not require someone who came to him wanting Islam to commit himself to prayer and zakāh. Indeed, it is narrated that he accepted Islam from a people who stipulated that they would not pay zakāh.

In the Musnad of Imam Aḥmad, Jābir said: Thaqīf stipulated to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that they would owe no charity and no jihād, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “They will give charity and they will fight in jihād.”
Also in it, from Naṣr ibn ʿĀṣim al-Laythī, from a man of their tribe: he came to the Prophet ﷺ and became Muslim on condition that he would pray only two prayers, and he accepted it from him.

Imam Aḥmad adopted these hadiths and said: Islam is valid with an invalid condition, and the person is then bound by all the laws of Islam. He also cited as evidence that Ḥakīm ibn Ḥizām said: I pledged allegiance to the Prophet ﷺ on condition that I would not go down [into prostration] except from standing.
Aḥmad said: It means that he would prostrate without bowing.
Muḥammad ibn Naṣr al-Marwazī recorded, with a very weak chain, that Anas said: The Prophet ﷺ would not accept anyone who answered his call to Islam except with the establishing of prayer
and the paying of zakāh; these were two obligations on whoever affirmed Muḥammad ﷺ and Islam.

That is the word of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: “Since you have not done so, and Allah has turned to you in forgiveness, establish the prayer and pay the zakāh” [al-Mujādilah 58:13]. This is not established; and even supposing it were, what it means is that he did not let anyone who entered Islam remain in it while abandoning prayer and zakāh — and that is true.

For when he ﷺ sent Muʿādh to Yemen he ordered him first to call them to the two testimonies, and said: “If they obey you in that, inform them of the prayer, then of zakāh.” What he meant is that whoever became a Muslim by entering Islam was then commanded to establish the prayer,

and then to pay zakāh. When someone asked him about Islam, he would mention to him the rest of Islam's pillars along with the two testimonies, as he did with Jibrīl (peace be upon him) when he asked him about Islam, and with the Bedouin with dishevelled hair who came asking about Islam.

What we have established shows how the wordings of the hadiths on this subject are to be reconciled, and makes clear that they are all true. The two words of testimony on their own protect whoever utters them, and by them he becomes a Muslim. Once he has entered Islam,

if he establishes the prayer, pays zakāh and carries out the laws of Islam, he has the rights of the Muslims and their obligations; and if he falls short in any of these pillars, then, if they are a group with the strength to resist, they are fought.
Some have thought that the hadith means the disbeliever is fought until he utters the two testimonies, establishes the prayer and pays zakāh,
and they made this a proof that disbelievers are addressed by the subsidiary rulings of the law. This is questionable; the practice of the Prophet ﷺ in fighting the disbelievers shows otherwise.
In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him): the Prophet ﷺ called ʿAlī on the day of Khaybar,

gave him the banner and said: “Go, and do not turn aside until Allah grants you victory.” ʿAlī went a little way, then stopped and called out: O Messenger of Allah, on what basis shall I fight the people?

He said: “Fight them until they testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah. If they do that, they have protected their blood and their wealth from you, except by its right,

and their reckoning is with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.” So he made the mere acceptance of the two testimonies a protection for lives and wealth, except by its right; and part of its right is refusing to pray and pay zakāh after entering Islam, as the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) understood.

Among the evidence from the Qurʾān that a group refusing to establish the prayer and pay zakāh is to be fought are His words, the Exalted: “But if they repent, establish the prayer and pay the zakāh, let them go their way” [al-Tawbah 9:5]; His words, the Exalted: “But if they repent, establish the prayer and pay the zakāh, they are your brothers in religion” [al-Tawbah 9:11]; and His words, the Exalted:

“Fight them until there is no more persecution and religion is for Allah” [al-Baqarah 2:193], taken together with His words, the Exalted: “They were commanded only to worship Allah, devoting religion sincerely to Him, as people of pure faith, and to establish the prayer and pay the zakāh; that is the upright religion” [al-Bayyinah 98:5].

It is established that when the Prophet ﷺ campaigned against a people, he would not attack them until morning: if he heard a call to prayer, [he held back]; otherwise he attacked them — even though it was possible that they had entered Islam.
He used to instruct his raiding parties: “If you hear a muʾadhdhin or see a mosque, do not kill anyone.”
He sent ʿUyaynah ibn Ḥiṣn against some people of Banū al-ʿAnbar, and he attacked them, having heard no call to prayer; they then claimed that they had become Muslim before that.
He ﷺ sent a letter to the people of ʿUmān which said: “From Muḥammad the Prophet to the people of ʿUmān: peace. To proceed:

affirm the testimony that there is no god but Allah and that I am the Messenger of Allah, pay zakāh and mark out mosques; otherwise I will campaign against you.” Al-Bazzār, al-Ṭabarānī and others recorded it.
All of this shows that he took into account the state of those entering Islam: if they established the prayer and paid zakāh, [well and good]; otherwise he did not refrain from fighting them.
It was over this that Abū Bakr and ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with them both) debated, as in the two Ṣaḥīḥs from Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said:

When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ died and Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq was made caliph after him, and those of the Arabs who disbelieved had disbelieved, ʿUmar said to Abū Bakr: How can you fight the people when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:
“I have been commanded to fight the people until they say ‘There is no god but Allah’. Whoever says ‘There is no god but Allah’

has protected his wealth and his life from me, except by its right, and his reckoning is with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic”? Abū Bakr said: By Allah, I will fight whoever separates prayer from zakāh, for zakāh is the right due on wealth.

By Allah, if they withheld from me a hobbling cord that they used to give to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, I would fight them for withholding it. ʿUmar said: By Allah, it was nothing other than that I saw that Allah had opened Abū Bakr's breast to fighting, and I knew that it was the truth.

Abū Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) derived fighting them from his words “except by its right”. This shows that fighting someone who utters the two testimonies is permissible by its right, and that part of its right is paying what is obligatory on wealth.

ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) thought that merely uttering the two testimonies protects one's blood in this world, holding to the general wording of the beginning of the hadith — just as some people have thought that whoever utters the two testimonies cannot enter the Fire in the Hereafter, holding to the general wording of certain texts.
But that is not how the matter stands. ʿUmar then came round to agreeing with Abū Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him).
Al-Nasāʾī recorded the story of Abū Bakr and ʿUmar's debate with an addition: that Abū Bakr said to ʿUmar: What the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said was only:
“I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god but Allah and that I am the Messenger of Allah, establish the prayer and pay the zakāh.”

Ibn Khuzaymah recorded it in his Ṣaḥīḥ; but ʿImrān al-Qaṭṭān erred in this narration, in both its chain and its text, as the leading ḥāfiẓ scholars said, among them ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī, Abū Zurʿah, Abū Ḥātim, al-Tirmidhī and al-Nasāʾī.
Neither Abū Bakr nor ʿUmar had this hadith from the Prophet ﷺ in this wording. Abū Bakr only said:
By Allah, I will fight whoever separates prayer from zakāh, for zakāh is the right due on wealth. He took this — and Allah knows best — from his words in the hadith, “except by its right”,

and in one narration, “except by the right of Islam”. So he counted establishing the prayer and paying zakāh as part of the right of Islam, just as not committing crimes that carry prescribed punishments is part of its right, and he took all of that to be among what was excepted by his words “except by its right”.
His saying, “I will fight whoever separates prayer from zakāh, for zakāh is the right due on wealth,” shows that whoever abandons prayer is to be fought,
because it is the right due on the body; and so too whoever abandons zakāh, which is the right due on wealth.
This indicates that fighting those who abandon prayer is a matter of consensus,

because he made it the base case from which the analogy was drawn, though it is not mentioned in the hadith ʿUmar cited as evidence; it was derived only from his words “except by its right”. So too with zakāh,
because it is part of its right; and all of these are among the rights of Islam.
Fighting over the abandonment of prayer is also shown by what is in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim from Umm Salamah, that the Prophet ﷺ said:

“Rulers will be appointed over you, and you will approve of some of what they do and disapprove of some. Whoever disapproves is free of blame, and whoever hates it is safe; but [not] whoever is pleased and follows.” They said: O Messenger of Allah, shall we not fight them?
He said: “No, so long as they pray.”
The ruling on those who abandon any of the pillars of Islam is that they are fought over it, just as they are fought for abandoning prayer and zakāh.
Ibn Shihāb narrated from Ḥanẓalah ibn ʿAlī ibn al-Asqaʿ that Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq sent Khālid ibn al-Walīd and ordered him to fight people over five things:

whoever abandoned one of the five, he was to fight him over it as he would fight over all five — the testimony that there is no god but Allah and that Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah, establishing the prayer, paying zakāh and fasting Ramaḍān.
Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb said: If people abandoned Ḥajj we would fight them over it, as we fight them over prayer and zakāh.
This, then, is the discussion of fighting a group that refuses any of these obligations.
As for executing an individual who refuses them, most scholars hold that one who refuses to pray is to be executed. This is the view of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad, Abū ʿUbayd and others.
It is shown by what is in the two Ṣaḥīḥs from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī: Khālid ibn al-Walīd asked the Prophet ﷺ for permission to kill a man, and he said:

“No; perhaps he prays.” Khālid said: How many a person who prays says with his tongue what is not in his heart! The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “I was not commanded to search people's hearts or to cut open their bellies.”
In the Musnad of Imam Aḥmad, from ʿUbaydullāh ibn ʿAdī ibn al-Khiyār: a man of the Anṣār told him that he came to the Prophet ﷺ and asked his permission to kill a man of the hypocrites.
The Prophet ﷺ said: “Does he not testify that there is no god but Allah?”
He said: Yes, but his testimony counts for nothing. He said: “Does he not pray?”
He said: Yes, but his prayer counts for nothing. He said: “Those are the ones Allah has forbidden me to kill.”
As for executing someone who refuses to pay zakāh, those who hold that one who refuses to perform the prayer is executed have two views on it.
The first is that he too is executed. This is the well-known position of Aḥmad, and this hadith of Ibn ʿUmar is cited as evidence for it.
The second is that he is not executed. This is the view of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and Aḥmad in one reported position.

As for fasting, Mālik, and Aḥmad in one reported position, said that one is executed for abandoning it; al-Shāfiʿī, and Aḥmad in another, said that one is not. Evidence for the latter view is the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar and others of the same meaning,
for none of them mentions fasting. That is why Aḥmad said, in the narration of Abū Ṭālib: Nothing has come concerning fasting.

I say: It has been narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, both as marfūʿ and as mawqūf (as the Prophet's words and as his own), that whoever abandons the two testimonies, the prayer or fasting is a disbeliever whose blood is lawful — unlike zakāh and Ḥajj.
It was mentioned earlier, in the commentary on the hadith “Islam is built on five”.

As for Ḥajj, there are two reported positions from Aḥmad on executing someone who abandons it. Some scholars of our school took the position that he is executed to refer to someone who delays it intending to abandon it altogether,
or delays it while thinking it most likely that he will die that year. If he delays it believing that it need not be performed at once, as many scholars hold, he is not executed for that.

His words ﷺ, “except by its right” — and in one narration “except by the right of Islam”: we have seen that Abū Bakr included in this right the performance of prayer and zakāh, and that some scholars included fasting and Ḥajj as well.

Part of its right is committing those forbidden acts that make a Muslim's blood lawful. Its right has been explained in this way in what al-Ṭabarānī and Ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī recorded from the hadith of Anas, that the Prophet ﷺ said:

“I have been commanded to fight the people until they say ‘There is no god but Allah’. When they say it, they have protected their blood and their wealth from me, except by its right, and their reckoning is with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.” He was asked: And what is its right?

He said: “Adultery after marriage, disbelief after faith, and killing a soul, for which one is killed.” Perhaps the end of it is the words of Anas; and it has been said that the correct view is that the whole hadith stops at him.
This is supported by what is in the two Ṣaḥīḥs from Ibn Masʿūd, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “The blood of a Muslim who testifies that there is no god but Allah

and that I am the Messenger of Allah is not lawful except in one of three cases: the married adulterer, a life for a life, and the one who abandons his religion and leaves the community.” This hadith will be discussed in full when it comes in its place in this book, if Allah the Exalted wills.

His words ﷺ, “and their reckoning is with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic,” mean that the two testimonies, together with establishing the prayer and paying zakāh, protect a person's blood and wealth in this world, unless he does something that makes his blood lawful.

In the Hereafter his reckoning is with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: if he was truthful, Allah will admit him to Paradise for it; if he was lying, he is one of the hypocrites in the lowest depth of the Fire.

We have already seen that some narrations in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim add: Then he recited: “So remind; you are only a reminder. You are not a controller over them — except whoever turns away and disbelieves: Allah will punish him with the greatest punishment. Indeed, to Us is their return; then indeed upon Us is their reckoning” [al-Ghāshiyah 88:21–26]. The meaning is:

your duty is only to remind them of Allah and call them to Him; you have not been given power to force faith into their hearts, nor are you charged with doing so. Then He said that the return of all servants is to Him and their reckoning rests with Him.
In the Musnad of al-Bazzār, from ʿIyāḍ al-Anṣārī, the Prophet ﷺ said: “‘There is no god but Allah’ is a word honoured with Allah;

it has a standing with Allah. Whoever says it truthfully, Allah will admit him to Paradise by it; and whoever says it falsely, it spares his wealth and his blood, and he will meet Allah tomorrow and He will call him to account.”

This is cited as evidence by those who hold that the repentance of the zindīq — the hypocrite — is accepted when he outwardly returns to Islam, and who do not hold that he is to be executed merely because his hypocrisy has come to light, just as the Prophet ﷺ dealt with the hypocrites

and treated them outwardly according to the rulings for Muslims, though he knew that some of them were hypocrites inwardly. This is the view of al-Shāfiʿī, and of Aḥmad in one reported position, and al-Khaṭṭābī reported it from most scholars. And Allah knows best.
